# Review without a queue: what Chen and Stratton (2026) mean for an autonomous system

*Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Abstract

Fiona Chen, James Stratton (Harvard University): AI coding tools raise code output substantially but final software output only a little, with no detectable employment effect. Code review becomes the bottleneck: code waits longer for a reviewer, spends longer in review and draws more requested changes. We map each of their findings to the mechanisms Ultrastable uses instead of a human review queue, and test each mapping against this system's own records. 5 of 7 are met today; each one that is not is an open work item with a closing probe, and this paper is regenerated from the measurements after every merge.

## 1. Introduction

A common view holds that AI writes more code, so a team must review more code, and review becomes the bottleneck. This paper tests a different account: review is a bottleneck only when a person is the gate. Replace the queue with checks that can fail, live verification and automatic revert, and measure quality instead of waiting.

We map each of their findings to the mechanisms Ultrastable uses instead of a human review queue, and test each mapping against this system's own records.

The question is narrow and testable. For each of 7 findings we name the concern, the mechanism in this system that is meant to answer it, and a metric from the system's own records that can show the answer does not hold. The findings cover economics, oversight, quality.

## 2. Background and related work

AI coding tools raise code output substantially but final software output only a little, with no detectable employment effect. Code review becomes the bottleneck: code waits longer for a reviewer, spends longer in review and draws more requested changes. [1]

Evidence base: 445M work events (GitHub, Jira, Google Calendar) for 720,542 workers at 655 firms, January 2021 to August 2026, from an engineering analytics platform; staggered difference-in-differences on AI tool adoption timing.

The design under test takes its name and its central mechanism from Ashby's ultrastable system [2]: a first feedback loop that acts on the world, and a second loop that changes the first loop's parameters only when an essential variable leaves its limits.

Ultrastable is that design as code [3]. Its loops, limits and ledgers are public, so each claim below can be checked against the files named.

## 3. Method

Metrics come from the system's own files: ops/research/prs.json (closed pull requests read from GitHub), ops/deploys.jsonl, ops/criticality.jsonl, ops/ultrastability.jsonl, doctrine/ultrastability.json, the loop registry and git history. Reproduce with `python3 -m foundation research --report`; every finding not met has a Q-RES item whose closing probe is `python3 -m foundation research --probe STUDY:F`.

Each finding is stated as a target on one metric, with a prediction logged before the measurement. A finding is met only when the measured value meets the target; a metric with no readings is reported as not measured, never as met.

## 5. Discussion

F1. More code is not more shipped work. After AI agent adoption, pull requests opened rise 35.7% while resolved issues (work deployed to production) rise only 13.7%; increases above 30.7% are ruled out. [1] In this system the answer is CRITICALITY-1 (the system's own score counts verified live deploys, never commits or lines); PROGRESS-1 (the public progress page lists merged and shipped work only; record-keeping merges are excluded). The metric, verified live deploys per merged pull request in the same window, reads 0.625 (n = 64) against a target of >= 0.5. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

F2. Review becomes the bottleneck. After AI agent adoption, the time from a pull request's submission to its merge rises 56.1%: waiting for a reviewer rises 59.9% and time in active review 58.5%. [1] In this system the answer is AUTO-SHIP-CLEAN-1 (a server-side lane merges a green pull request without waiting for a person); HANDOFF-1 (the tick Worker owns merge, deploy and live verification after a pull request opens); DRAIN-ZERO-1 (a green pull request left open fails a check). The metric, median hours from a pull request opening to its merge, reads 0.15 (n = 64) against a target of <= 1.0. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

F3. System-made changes wait longer than session-made ones. The study's model predicts that when review capacity is fixed, the waiting time grows with the volume of submitted code. A system that writes its own changes must not let its own pull requests queue behind human-driven ones. [1] In this system the answer is DRAIN-ALL-1 (the lane takes every open pull request until none is left); SELF-REFERENCE-1 (work the system originates on itself is ranked first when the regime is driven). The metric, median hours to merge for pull requests the system's own workflows or App opened, reads 0.49 (n = 13) against a target of <= 2.0. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

F4. Lower code quality raises review effort and risk. After agent adoption the share of changes receiving a review comment rises 13.1% and comments per change rise 38.6%; interviewees report outages caused by AI-generated commits. [1] In this system the answer is ELISION-1 (a model change that elides or stubs code is refused before it becomes a pull request); REDMAIN-1 (a red main is repaired by reverting the smallest change that broke it); FAILURE-RESOLVE-1 (every failure mode has a live detector and a queue item). The metric, commits on main whose subject starts with Revert, per merged pull request in the window, reads 0.0 (n = 64) against a target of <= 0.05. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

F5. Unverified deploys reach production. Code must be reviewed and tested before it can be deployed; the study treats review as the quality gate that AI-written code strains. [1] In this system the answer is HANDOFF-1 (every deploy runs a verify line against production and rolls back on failure); FRONT-BACKED-1 (freshness of each live source is served and probed). The metric, share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit, reads 1.0 (n = 40) against a target of >= 0.95. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

F6. AI review tools leave humans in the loop. 79.1% of firms adopted AI code review tools, but the overwhelming majority of reviews and comments are still written by people, so the bottleneck persists. [1] In this system the answer is CLOSED-LOOP-1 (no step waits on a person reading, reviewing or approving); CRITICALITY-1 (human touches are counted every tick and lower the score). The metric, share of merged pull requests opened by the system itself, reads 0.203 (n = 64) against a target of >= 0.5. The mechanism does not yet hold; work item Q-RES-chen-stratton-2026-F6 carries the fix and closes only when the same measurement passes.

F7. One approver is a single point of failure. Reviewers mostly review code they already know (82.8% versus 17.2% at random); an interviewee describes one senior engineer as the only approver, reviewing once a week. [1] In this system the answer is GUIDING-DIRECTIVE section 12 (every single point of failure, approvals included, is registered and remediated); NO-SINGLE-ROUTE (every merge and deploy path has a second route needing no person's credential). The metric, verified deploys the system originated and executed itself (latest criticality tick), reads 0 (n = 0) against a target of >= 1. The mechanism does not yet hold; work item Q-RES-chen-stratton-2026-F7 carries the fix and closes only when the same measurement passes.

## 6. Limitations

- Scale. One organization: 100 closed pull requests (64 merged) over 0.75 days, against a study of 655 firms over more than five years. Our numbers describe this system; they are not a causal estimate and are not compared with the study's effect sizes as if they were.
- Who wrote the changes. 80% of merged pull requests in the window were opened by code agent sessions run under the owner's account, not by the system's own loops. The latest criticality tick puts the system in the subcritical regime with 0 self-originated deploys, so most of the work measured here was started from outside.
- Review by construction. Ultrastable has no human review step, so a short open-to-merge time is partly a consequence of the design. The real test of the design is quality: the revert and deploy-verification findings, which can fail.
- Revert share counts commits whose subject starts with Revert; a fix that undoes a change without that word is not counted, so the figure is a lower bound.
- Source. Job market paper (working paper, not peer reviewed), version 2026-11-19 (first version 2026-01-07); its findings may change in later versions.

## 7. Conclusion

On this system's records, 5 of 7 findings hold. The gaps are ai review tools leave humans in the loop; one approver is a single point of failure.

That is evidence against the view that more AI code means a bigger human review queue: the properties tested here are engineering properties of the loop, and each can be measured and repaired without waiting on a better model.

The paper is regenerated from the measurements after every merge, so a reader who returns later sees the current result, not this one.
